name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: Board advisory and fiduciary risk in AI covers the duties of corporate directors when overseeing artificial intelligence use and strategy. It includes advising boards on AI opportunities and threats, setting oversight structures, and ensuring directors meet their duties of care and loyalty. The scope also takes in the risk that directors face personal liability for failing to oversee AI-related harms, such as privacy breaches, discrimination, or intellectual property infringement. This work sits at the intersection of corporate governance, regulatory compliance, and technology risk management.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on the board's committee structure, typically audit, risk, and technology or innovation committees, supported by management reporting lines. It relies on board portals for secure document sharing, governance, risk, and compliance platforms for tracking issues, and sometimes specialized AI governance tools for inventory and impact assessments. Legal and compliance teams provide the underlying data, including AI use case registers, incident reports, and regulatory updates. External advisors and counsel may also feed into the board's information flow.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through regular board briefings, risk assessments, and oversight reviews that map AI use cases to legal and ethical risks. Directors may ask management to conduct AI impact assessments, review vendor contracts for data rights, and monitor regulatory changes. Advisors often use frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to structure discussions, and they document oversight decisions to show that duties were met. The method also includes tabletop exercises for AI incidents and periodic reviews of AI policies and controls.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here center on fiduciary duties, disclosure obligations, and the provenance of data used in AI systems. Boards must weigh intellectual property exposure, privacy rights, and the risk of biased outcomes, all of which can lead to litigation or regulatory action. The site tracks 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which illustrate the kinds of disputes that can inform board risk assessments. Provenance matters because directors may need to know where training data came from and whether it was lawfully obtained. Governance also covers director indemnification, D&O insurance, and the documentation of oversight efforts.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more formal AI oversight as a fiduciary expectation, with boards adding AI expertise and standing committees. Regulatory activity is expanding, and the site tracks 6940 state AI bills, which suggests a growing patchwork of rules that boards will need to monitor. We can expect more guidance from regulators and stock exchanges on AI disclosure and risk management. Insurance markets may also adapt with new products for AI-related director liability. Over time, board advisory may shift from ad hoc briefings to continuous, data-driven oversight of AI systems.
